who: MEX/Veracruz de Ignacio de la Llave
name: Veracruz de Ignacio de la Llave
summary_text: Veracruz led the national LGBT+ fatality count for four consecutive years — in 2021 alone, 10 recorded violent deaths of LGBT+ people, ahead of Guanajuato (9), Estado de México (7) and Chihuahua (6), with 19 of 32 states recording victims that year. In 2025 the state closed the year with at least 15 hate crimes against the LGBT+ community; a January 2025 running total put 460 hate-crime cases unresolved, and Emblematic cases have arrests but no final sentences. Activists cite 'rezago y archivamiento de expedientes' (deliberate filing-away of cases), and the state prosecutor's office has lost investigative files entirely; in one emblematic case (a chef killed in February 2021) the family reported that the homicide file had simply disappeared, and organisers call the 2025 pride march a platform against that impunity. The killing of 'Luis M', a 27-year-old trans woman stabbed to death in a motel in Oluta on 19 November 2025, came after the state observatory had already counted 9 hate crimes earlier that year, three of them against trans women; the Coatzacoalcos-Oluta corridor is named in the national notes as Veracruz's concentration zone. The danger inside the state is metro-and-corridor concentrated rather than uniform. The only institutional counterweight is recent: Veracruz passed its gender-identity civil-code reform in 2025 with no age limit, among the last to legislate one (2025): 22 of 32 states had a procedure by March 2025. Before that, a visitor or resident had no legal route to correct documents. The absence of any functioning investigation or prosecution machinery — distinct from other states where laws exist but enforcement is weak — makes the impunity here total. Context for comparison: Guanajuato, which carries sustained violence too, has a comprehensive diversity law and a court-forced recognition procedure; Nayarit typified the transfeminicide offence first in the country (March 2024). Veracruz's four-year lethality record combined with explicit case-archiving and lost files represents the worst enforcement climate, and its legal framework arrived latest and is least functional.

sources.claim_summary: Letra S 'Muertes violentas de personas LGBT+ en México — Informe 2021' (May 2022): Veracruz led the national count of violent deaths of LGBT+ people for the fourth consecutive year, with 10 recorded cases in 2021, followed by Guanajuato (9), Estado de México (7) and Chihuahua (6); 19 of 32 states recorded victims. The report notes under-reporting: in a third of 2021 cases no name was published, and in 43 percent the sex recorded was male without attention to gender identity.

sources.title: Veracruz cerró 2025 con 15 crímenes de odio contra la comunidad LGBTQ+ - Diario de Xalapa
sources.claim_summary: Diario de Xalapa (4 Feb 2026): Veracruz closed 2025 with 15 hate crimes against the LGBT+ community — a 'whitewash' year for authorities, say organisations; Orgullo Xalapa activists keep the count visible because the problem receives little official visibility. Related state coverage names Martinez de la Torre, Minatitan and Coatepec as the municipalities with most displacement from insecurity, and records one community homicide (Guillermo Pamuce Yep, Coatzacoalcos) whose investigation a state party asked the federal attorney general to take over.

sources.title: Crímenes de odio contra la comunidad LGBTTQI en Veracruz, sin resolver - La Jornada Veracruz
sources.claim_summary: La Jornada Veracruz (2025, interview with Orgullo Xalapa network activist Leonardo Ruiz): 460 hate-crime cases against the LGBT+ community remain unresolved in the state; murder files have gone missing inside the attorney general's office (FGE) — the case of chef Miguel Ángel Sulvarán Xolo (killed 13 Feb 2021) with a lost file; suspects in another case left the country without ever being charged; of ten cases only one or two are resolved and under 20 percent end with a conviction or an imprisoned perpetrator; families report revictimisation at the FGE; Veracruz is 'third place' in hate crimes; organisers call the march demand for justice 'a platform' against impunity; the state human-rights commission head was named march honouree.
